The transformer architecture [attention2017] revolutionised NLP. Building on this, BERT [bert2019] introduced bidirectional training.
Studying the chemical interactions is important for understanding the reality around us. Everything, from stars to viruses, is an equilibrium between an intricate physical-chemical reaction network, where a small change in one of its produces extreme consequences for all others.

In this website I will guide you trough my journey into exploring different topics of computational astrochemistry. We will see:
the role fo water ice surfaces in the interstellar medium as a catalyst for the formation of molecules, looking at $\ce{O2}$ as an example; the modellisation of photodissociation of diatomic and triatomic molecules, as a way to produce data that are essential to simulate conditions varying from the cold space between starts, to their hot surfaces; the study of non reactive scattering of diatomic molecules with atoms and other diatomics, as they can promote relaxation of newly formed species or enhance reactivity exciting the molecules involved in the reaction. Surface reactivity# The outcome of a chemical reaction is highly dependent on the conditions in which it takes place. Changes in thermodynamic conditions, like temperature and pressure, are known to inhibit or enhance the yield of a reaction, to favour the reactant or the product state. Another important role is played by the environment surrounding the reactive species. When going from the gas phase to the bulk phase the diffusivity and number of reactive species are inversely proportional. In solid and liquids the presence of an electric field, generated by the difference of electron density of the other molecules, modifies the reaction path.
Reactions that take place in heterogeneous environments occur at the interface (or surface) between two different phases (solid-liquid, solid-gas, liquid-liquid, etc). The interface is defined as the boundary between two spatial regions occupied by different types of matter or by matter in different states. The physico-chemical properties at the interface cannot be inferred by the simple combination of the single phases from which it is originated as phase changes causes unpredictable variation in the system.
Surfaces are important because they can act as catalysts for chemical reactions. They are particularly efficient catalysts, they are able not only to reduce reaction barriers, but they can also trap particles in cavities, facilitating the encounter of the reactive species and they can stabilize the newly formed molecules. An example of surface catalysed process are the association/dissociation of small molecules on top of surfaces, especially in photochemical and electrochemical processes.
In real systems the components of an interface are often irregular or even amorphous as there is a loss or even a complete lack of symmetry or homogeneity elements. These irregularities can be physical, like the presence of cavities, pores and terraces, or chemical, meaning that the surface is composed of different species. For example an amorphous surface is formed when solidification processes happens too quickly for the atoms to rearrange themselves.
Water as a surface# Water is one of the most ubiquitous molecules in nature as it is found from space to inside organisms. Despite being a quite simple molecule composed of two hydrogen and an oxygen atom, water chemistry is different from all other chemical compounds, making it one of the main actors in chemistry. In both liquid and gas phase, $\ce{H2O}$ is characterized by an extensive hydrogen bond (H-bond) network, in which a hydrogen atom is placed between two oxygen atoms. The high directionality of the H-bonds and the average bond strength of 5 kcal/mol[1] means that they are the predominant forces in the inter-molecular interactions. This strength derives from the high polarization along the oxygen-hydrogen bond and consequently the $\ce{H2O}$ molecules needs to be explicitly treated in computational simulations.

title: The chemistry of the interstellar medium
content:
The interstellar medium# In all galaxies, the space between celestial bodies is filled with a collection of gas and dust particles. These particles are known as interstellar medium (ISM) and possesses density of $10^{-9}$ grains$\times$cm$^{-3}$.\citep{wakelamrev} The ISM plays an important role as a reservoir of constituents for the formation of new stars. ISM is mostly composed of hydrogen atoms and they are used to measure the relative abundances of the other elements. The second most common element is helium with a relative abundance of 8.5$\times 10^{-2}$ per hydrogen atom, followed by oxygen (2.6$\times 10^{-4}$per hydrogen atom\citep{Markwick_2000}) and carbon (1.2$\times 10^{-4}$ \citep{cardelli_1993} per hydrogen atom). All other elements are present with abundances lower than $10^{-4}$.
The ISM floats in a sea of electromagnetic and particle radiations. Massive stars are the main sources of ultraviolet and visible radiation, and after absorption and re-emission by dust, they create a strong infrared field. Novae and supernovae are sources of high energy X-ray and $\gamma$-ray radiation. Cosmic rays are fast-moving atomic nuclei (mostly protons) with average energies of the order of a few MeV. They are the only particles able to penetrate into the denser dusty regions and ionize the H$_2$ molecule. The subsequent ion-electron recombination is then responsible for the weak ultraviolet radiation field inside the dust itself.
Most of the interstellar volume is occupied by \ce{H^+} ions, with a density of 10$^{-3}$ particle $\times $cm$^{-3}$ at a temperature of 10$^6$ K. This gas surrounds cooler regions with temperatures of $T\leq$ 300 K, where chemical processes are possible and the destruction *via} UV-photodissociation is suppressed. The *diffuse clouds} are the first of those regions: the presence of dust grain carried with gas provides a defence against the interstellar radiation field. More complex processes are observed in the *translucent clouds}, where the large density (1000 particle$\times$cm$^{-3}$) shields the inner regions against starlight from massive stars. In the *molecular clouds} the high energy photons are completely extinguished by the concentration of dust grains. The density of particles increase by an order of magnitude and the temperature decreases up to 10 K: under these conditions molecules are the main components in gas phase or in the form of ice.
The interaction between the ISM dust and a star was observed by Edward Piggot in 1796\citep{pigott1797}: he discovered that the star R Coronae Borealis fades from its normal brightness for a period of months or sometimes years on irregular intervals. The presence of dust was later confirmed by direct imaging with the Hubble Space Telescope which observed an extensive dust cloud out to a radius around 2000 astronomical units (1 astronomical unit is equal to $150 \times 10^6$ km) from the star\citep{hubble2012rcoronae}. The first direct measurements of dust in the heliosphere were carried by the Ulysses mission and later by the Galileo mission\citep{landgraf2000}: grain of the range from between 10$^{-15}$ to more than 10$^{-10}$ grams were observed.
In order to speculate about the chemical composition of the dust in the ISM, it is helpful to consider the *elemental depletion} for each element: their underabundance is estimated with respect to the chemical composition in the gas phase of a hot star’s atmosphere. It was noted that, for example, oxygen in gaseous species and in silica and metal oxides does not account for all the assumed abundance\citep{Whittet_2010}. #{The role of interestellar dust} The molecular clouds are “giant laboratories”, in which the interactions between gas and solid particles at ultra low pressure and temperatures for long timescales enables solid state and surface chemistry which are inaccessible in terrestrial experiments. The dusts provide the surface on which heterogeneous chemistry occurs and it is a substrate on which the icy mantles grow.
ISM molecular species can be formed through a network of gas phase reactions. The basic radiative association of two atoms under interstellar conditions is strongly forbidden by quantum mechanical selection rules, however three body association is possible. The problem is that the interstellar particle density is many order of magnitudes lower than the critical value needed for making those processes efficient, with the purely gas-phase networks failing to provide a mechanism that gives reasonable abundances of molecular species detected in interstellar clouds in star forming regions.
For those molecules surface chemistry plays a crucial role. In case of a diatomic reaction, a first atom collides with an interstellar grain and is retained on the surface until a second atom arrives and reacts with it. This scenario constrains the possible reaction conditions: the first atom will have to stick to the grain surface and be retained sufficiently long to encounter the second atom and before desorption processes takes place. In the case where both atom are physisorbed and thermalized with the surface, the reaction takes place *via} the *Langmuir-Hinshelwood} mechanism\citep{langmuir1922}, or an excited atom can arrive at the surface near to an adsorbed atom and a bond can be formed *via} the *Eley-Rideal} mechanism\citep{cuppenhornek2008}. The “hot atom mechanism”\citep{hotatom} is an intermediate process: thermal accommodation can occur through repeated interactions with the surface in which the kinetic energy of the atom is successively reduced.
In those reactions, the primary role of the surface is to transfer energy from the hindered vibration-rotation of nascent molecule into the other modes. The energy can flow to the translational modes, leading to the desorption of a rovibrationally excited molecule. Alternatively, the nascent molecule may be weakly trapped in an excited state from which it will be later released or react with other species on the grain.
The presence of dust is important both in star and planet formation. Star formation begins in cold, dark, dense molecular clouds, shielded from the interstellar radiation field. If the cloud has a sufficient mass, it may become unstable due to gravitational collapse, the grains help quenching the heat generated during the process and, once the critical mass is reached and the temperature in the star-forming region begins to rise, they participate to the planet formation stage. This involves collision between grains, driven by Van der Waals forces and kinetic collisions, that may lead to the compaction of loosely formed structures.
#{The interstellar ice } Most of the grain surfaces are covered by *ice}, mostly H$_2$O (with a density of 1000 molecule$\times$ cm$^{-3}$)\citep{watreview2013} with traces of other small species (i.e CH$_4$, NH$_3$,CH$_3$OH,CO,CO$_2$,N$_2$, *etc})\citep{Gibb_2004}. Water ice is detected by its absorption in the pure O-H stretching mode in a broad feature peaking near 3 $\mu$m and by the bending and the combination of libration modes from 4.5-6.3 $\mu$m\citep{gillett1973}. In the ISM the ice is detected in the foreground material observed against a cool background star that has a prominent infrared continuum spectrum. Most of the detected ice seems to be in a high density amorphous form that has a sharp laboratory spectral feature at 3.1 $\mu$m. Porous ice has a feature at 2.7 $\mu$m originating in a dangling OH bond, that is is not detected, suggesting its rarity in the ISM\citep{accolla2011}. The presence of impurities modifies the central position and line profiles of pure water ice features.
Ice is inferred to be formed by the sticking of O atoms to the grain surface, and their hydrogenation and retention as water molecules. Chemical pathways to form water ice may also include hydrogenation of O$_2$ and O$_3$, formed as well on the surface. In gas phase chemistry, water formation is hindered by the presence of carbon that takes up all the oxygen it can. % For this reason, CO is the most abundant molecule after H$_2$.
The absence of ice in low extinction regions of interstellar space and the inhibition of ice deposition in them are still not fully understood but it must depend on the balance between various desorption processes and the incidence of O atoms at the grain surface. Within all the possible desorption processes on the grain surface, thermal desorption, photodesorption by UV-radiations, interaction with cosmic rays and local heating by other surface reactions are hypothesized to be the most prominent.
The interaction between a solitary water molecule and the surface of a bare grain is different to that of a water molecule that is part of a monolayer: in the first case the molecule simply binds with the surface while in the latter the binding is enhanced by H-bonding to adjacent water molecules. This finding is confirmed by experiments which showed that by increasing the H$_2$O coverage molecules desorb at higher temperatures\citep{cazaux2010}. In the cloud’s dense regions a water monolayer tends to build up due to the flux of O atoms incident on the grain surfaces and hydrogen bonding among the molecule constituents dominates most desorption process and ensures ice mantel growth on the initial monolayer.
Amorphous ice, known as amorphous solid water (ASW), is formed if the atoms on the surface are frozen and their diffusion on the surface is smaller than the lattice constant of the crystalline form of ice. The diffusion coefficient (*D}) of amorphous solid water is larger than hexagonal ice I$_h$ by one or two order of magnitude at the temperatures where ASW is preserved. The crystallization time scale estimated at 10 K is much larger than the cloud lifetime of 10$^7$ years. In our solar system the conditions for preserving ASW are found outside the Saturnian region\citep{kouchi1994}.
Due to the different conditions in different clouds, the polymorphs of water are relevant for ISM thermodynamical conditions. While the amorphous ice dominates below 130 K, metastable cubic phase (I$_c$) is formed at $130 < T< 170$ K, while I$_h$ forms a stable phase at $T > 170$ K \citep{hobbs1974}. Figure \ref{fig:ices} displays the three different surfaces. Crystallization is enhanced by the presence of UV photons, producing a cycle of formation-dissociation-formation through exothermic reactions\citep{cazaux2010}. This excess of energy can be redistributed to the grain, starting a local nucleation processes. \begin{figure} \begin{center} \includegraphics[scale=0.25]{introduction/figures/ices.pdf} \end{center} \caption{Representation of the water ice surface for the three different polymorphs: ASW (left), I$_c$ (center) and I$_h$ (right).} \label{fig:ices} \end{figure}
#{Water formation} In the molecular clouds the observed abundance of water ice cannot be explained by the direct accretion of gas phase only. In gas phase it ranges from $n_{\textrm{\ce{H2O}}}< 10^{-8}$ in the coldest clouds to $n_{\textrm{\ce{H2O}}}> 10^{-4}$ in warm gas and shocks \citep{bergin1998,hollenbach2008}. This observation suggests the formation and successive evaporation of ice from the surface.
H$_2$O formation channels strongly depend on the local environment in the interstellar cloud\citep{Cuppen_2007}. Heavy atoms (in this case defined as atoms heavier than He) are deposited on top of carbonaceous and silicate grains, while the incoming H atom is trapped and diffuses into the surface with a temperature dependent efficiency. The involvement of the \ce{O} atom is the main route in the translucent and diffuse clouds, while the \ce{O2} and the \ce{O3} route are more efficient in cold molecular clouds. In those clouds the grain surface should be covered by different monolayers of amorphous solid \ce{O2} and temperature programmed desorption experiments show that hydrogen can penetrate the surface\citep{cuppenioppolo2010-1,cuppenioppolo2010-2}. This penetration can be addressed by different factors, for example the high mobility of O$_2$ when temperature is increased, crystallization of O$_2$, replenishment of the oxygen molecule on top of the surface and thermal activation of H. Below 10 K water formation is dominated by hydrogen diffusion, while from $T > 30 $ K strongly physisorbed oxygen atoms can diffuse and encounter other species\citep{cazaux2010}. The \ce{H2O} reaction network leading to water formation is pictured in Figure \ref{fig:cuppenioppolo2010-2} from Ref\citep{cuppenioppolo2010-2}. \begin{figure} \begin{center} \includegraphics[scale=1.00]{introduction/figures/cuppen.pdf} \end{center} \caption{Oxygen chemical reaction network proposed by Cuppen et *al} in Ref\citep{cuppenioppolo2010-2} (represented in Figure 5 in the article). They found four different reaction types: barrierless reactions (solid), reactions with a barrier but with detectable efficiency (dashed), reactions with efficiency below the experimental detection limit (dash-dotted), and undetermined efficiency reactions (dotted). The light gray arrows indicate the same entering channel but with different outgoing channels, and the black arrows are the reactions of the original reaction scheme.} \label{fig:cuppenioppolo2010-2} \end{figure}
#{The chemistry of oxygen} Due to the role of oxygen in water formation and its abundance, its evolution over the life of molecular cloud is the key to understand its development. Oxygen bearing species can be divided into two categories, the first typology, like \ce{H2O}, whose maximum abundance in gas phase is reached before getting to the cloud’s steady state ($\sim$ 10$^5$-10$^6$ years) and the second in which the maximum abundance is reached at the steady state, as CO and \ce{O2}. The great majority of atomic oxygen is trapped in CO with a relative abundance of 10$^{-4}$ with respect to \ce{H2} reached around 10$^5$ years\citep{wakelamrev} after the cloud formation.
Molecular oxygen is an important component for the formation of \ce{H2O}, via the \ce{H2O2} and \ce{O3} channels \citep{Ioppolo2008}. A strong correlation between \ce{H2O} and \ce{O2} abundance is found in the 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko cometary coma\citep{bieler2015abundant}. O$_2$ has long been unsuccessfully predicted as the most abundant species in cold dense clouds and was recently detected in the warm region of the $\rho$-Ophiuchi cloud\citep{o2obs2007,o2obs2012} with an abundance of $5 \times 10^{-8}$ relative to H$_2$. The same abundance is estimated for cold molecular clouds\citep{o2estimate2003}. The difficulties in its identification are due to the \ce{O2} being infrared inactive: only when the molecule is embedded in a matrix a detection of the vibrational mode at 1551 cm$^{-1}$ can be achieved\citep{caselli2018}. The most probable reason for the mismatch between predictions and observations is the adsorption of \ce{O2} on the surface. This hypothesis is supported by the evidence of intermediate species involved in water formation network\citep{cuppenioppolo2010-2} (HO$_2$ and H$_2$O$_2$) in the $\rho$-Ophiuchi cloud. Other possible causes such as very young or carbon rich clouds are ruled out due to their specific conditions\citep{Markwick_2000}.
In gas phase, the main proposed reaction for the formation of O$_2$ is\citep{davidsson1990,carty2006}: \begin{equation} \ce{OH + O -> O2 + H}. \end{equation} In solid phase O$_2$ the two following formation mechanism have been proposed:% competes with the %\begin{equation} % \ce{CO +O -> CO2} %\end{equation} %reaction\citep{ioppolo2011} and the the following formation paths have been proposed: \begin{equation} \ce{O + O -> O2} \end{equation} and
\begin{equation} \ce{HO2 + H -> O2 + H2 }, \end{equation} with the first\citep{ioppolo2011} preferred to the second, due to the high activation barrier (19.0 kcal/mol)\citep{Mousavipour2007} of the latter. Oxygen formation through decomposition of \ce{H2O2} does not seem to be an efficient mechanism, due to the lower efficiency of the reaction in respect to what would be needed for explaining astrochemical models\citep{dulieu2017}.
An important factor for the oxygen atom reactivity is the study of the surface diffusion mechanism. It is observed that diffusion can only occur on the top of the surface as crossing the first water bulk layer should take 10$^{29}$ s, making this process impossible\citep{minissale2019}. The diffusion energy ($E_{\textrm{dif}}$) is estimated by temperature desorption experiments from the desorption energy ($E_{\textrm{des}}$) by the following expression: \begin{equation} E_{\textrm{dif}}= 0.7 E_{\textrm{des}} \end{equation} From $E_{\textrm{des}} \sim 1320$ K, it derived that $E_{\textrm{dif}} \sim 750$ K\citep{minissale2016}. Temperature desorption experiments from 6-25 K show that the measured diffusion does not follow a typical Arrhenius form: \begin{equation}\label{eq:introarrh} D = D_0 \exp \left( \frac{ E_\textrm{dif}}{k_BT}\right) \end{equation} with $D_0$ as Arrhenius constant, and $k_{\textrm{B}}$ the Boltzmann constant. Possible tunneling quantum effects below 20 K were supposed to be responsible for diffusion enhancement.
The combination of two oxygen atoms in their ground states ($^3$P) generates \ce{O2} in different electronic state, and each of them in various possible vibrational states\citep{ogilvie:2018}. The first ($^1\Delta_g$) and second ($^1\Sigma_g^+$) excited states are known for their higher reactivity compared to the ground state. In the gas phase the transition $a^1\Delta_g \rightarrow$ $X^3\Sigma_g^-$ is both spin and symmetry forbidden and $b^1 \Sigma_g^+ \rightarrow$ $X^3\Sigma_g^-$ is spin forbidden, with radiative lifetimes of 4000 s and 150 s, induced by magnetic-dipole and electric-quadrupole interactions\citep{parker:2014} respectively. However, forbidden transitions can occur in the presence of an environment that breaks the molecular symmetry. Relaxation from the $^1\Sigma_g^+$ state to $^3\Sigma_g^-$ occurs *via} Inter System Crossing (ISC), governed by Spin Orbit Coupling (SOC) that can be described using the Landau Zener formalism\citep{wodtke:1999,minaev2003,dayou2005}.
